result:
The kitchen window is the size of a single palm, the one on the left hand, the one you'd press flat against a door before opening it. That's the exact scale of the glass. And right now, in the grey half-hour before the sun decides whether it's going to show up, rain is doing its slow, stupid, beautiful work against the pane. One drop forms in a groove where the glass hasn't been cleaned in three weeks. It swells, tugs at the surface tension, and finally lets go. It drags a thin silver thread down the window, crossing the path of two other drops that are still hanging there, still deciding. One of them, a smaller one, gets swallowed into the bigger trail and vanishes. The other survives, shrunken, tilted sideways, and keeps its own path.

I've been watching this for eleven minutes. I know because I set my phone face-down on the counter with the screen lit up, counting, and then I lost track and started again, and then I lost track again, and now it's eleven minutes or maybe nine. The exact number doesn't matter. What matters is that I am *here*, in this kitchen, in this particular Tuesday, and the rain is not going to care if I'm watching it. The rain will do what it does. But the watching is a small act of refusal. Refusal to be the version of me that's already in the car, already thinking about the meeting, already three hours ahead in a life that feels like a conveyor belt where you're the box and the belt is the morning and the destination is somewhere you've already been.

My grandmother used to sit by the kitchen window. Not a window this small. Hers was wider, the kind with a little shelf inside that held a cracked ceramic bowl of sugar packets and a pen that never worked properly. She'd sit with her tea going cold, and she'd watch the street, and people who knew her would say she was watching for nothing. But I remember now, pressing my face against her kitchen chair's edge, that she wasn't watching for nothing. She was watching for the way the light changed. The way the shadows of the elms on the sidewalk stretched and contracted like slow breathing. The way a dog would stop mid-stride, lift its nose, and commit to a smell so fully that the rest of the walk became irrelevant for ten seconds. She was watching the world do its small, specific things, and she was letting them be small and specific. She wasn't extracting meaning. She wasn't building a narrative. She was just *present* in the most undramatic, un-Instagrammable way, and it made her look, to me, like the only person in the house who was actually alive rather than just occupying the shape of a person.

I miss that. I miss watching rain without recording it. I miss the fact that no one would have asked what I was getting out of it. There was no prompt. No assignment. No one to tell me the rain was a metaphor for grief or transition or the passage of time. The rain was just wet air falling from a cloud. And that was enough. That was the whole thing. The wet air falling.

Now I'm thirty-seven and I keep trying to make the rain into a story. I think, *this is where the scene where I finally call my mother could happen.* I think, *the grey light is my emotional state.* I think, *the three drops on the window represent the three decisions I've been avoiding this week.* And I catch myself doing this and I feel a small, warm embarrassment, like I've been caught wearing an outfit that's a little too try-hard. The rain doesn't need me to make it mean something. The rain just needs to fall, and the glass just needs to be cold, and the thread of water just needs to follow the groove that's already there.

The sun comes up. Not all at once. A thin pale line first, at the top of the window, like someone sliding a letter under a door. Then the line thickens. The grey in the kitchen shifts, warms, takes on a faint yellow. The drops on the glass catch it and suddenly they're not just drops. They're tiny, crooked lanterns. The one that survived the merge is now a bright, trembling point, and I think, *yes, that's beautiful*, and then I think, *I already said that about the rain last week, in my journal, in almost exactly the same words*, and I feel the faintest pang of redundancy, of a mind that has circled the same small observation so many times that the grooves are wearing deep.

But I keep watching. The sun gets higher. The drops are almost dry now, leaving a faint mineral film behind, a ghost of where they were. The window is clear for a few minutes. Then a new drop forms, in a different groove this time, because the rain hasn't stopped, it's just gotten lighter, thinner, more patient. It swells. It tugs. It lets go.

I drink my coffee. It's cold. I drink it anyway.

The kitchen is the size of the kitchen. The window is the size of a palm. The rain is doing its slow, stupid, beautiful work, and I am here, and no one is asking me what it all means, and for eleven more minutes, or nine, or whatever, that is enough. That is the whole thing. The wet air falling. The thread following the groove. The small, crooked lantern catching a light it didn't ask for and holding it, just for a second, before the sun moves on and the glass goes clear again and the whole small drama starts over in a new groove, a new path, a new small death and new small beginning that no one will ever see.

I set the phone down. I don't flip it over. I leave it face-up on the counter, screen dark now, reflecting the window, reflecting the rain, reflecting the thin yellow line of a morning that isn't a metaphor, isn't a transition, isn't a scene from a novel I'm halfwriting in my head. Just a morning. Just water on glass. Just the particular, unrepeatable weight of this Tuesday pressing down on the tile floor and into the soles of my bare feet.

I stay. I watch the new drop. I let it be nothing. I let it be everything it is, which is a drop of water on a window, in a kitchen, in a life that is not a conveyor belt, not a story, not a prompt. Just a Tuesday. Just rain. Just the long, slow, stupid, beautiful work of being here while the light changes, and changes, and changes, until the grey is gone and the whole small world outside the window is just the world, ordinary and enormous and utterly indifferent to the fact that I am watching it, and somehow, for eleven minutes, that indifference is the most generous thing it could offer.
